}}'''David M. Young Jr.''' (October 20, 1923 – December 21, 2008<ref>{{cite news | title=Dr. David M. Young Jr. | url=http://www.legacy.com/statesman/Obituaries.asp?Page=Lifestory&PersonId=121811293 | work=[[Austin American-Statesman]] | date=2008-12-25 | accessdate=25 December 2008}}</ref>) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[computer scientist]] who was one of the pioneers in the field of modern [[applied mathematics|numerical analysis/scientific computing]].

==Contributions==
Young is best known for establishing the mathematical framework for iterative methods (a.k.a. [[preconditioner|preconditioning]]). These [[algorithms]] are now used in computer software on high performance supercomputers for the numerical solution of large [[Sparse matrix|sparse linear systems]] arising from problems involving [[partial differential equations]]. See, in particular, the [[successive over-relaxation]] (SOR) and [[symmetric successive over-relaxation]] (SSOR) methods.<ref name="nlaa95">{{citation | title = Editorial
 | first1 = Owe | last1 = Axelsson | first2 = Yuri A. | last2 = Kuznetsov
 | journal = Numerical Linear Algebra with Applications
 | volume = 2 | issue = 5 | page = 399 | year = 1995 | doi = 10.1002/nla.1680020502| doi-access = free }}.</ref>

When Young first began his research on [[iterative methods]] in the late 1940s, there was some skepticism with the idea of using iterative methods on the new computing machines to solve industrial-size problems. Ever since Young's ground-breaking Ph.D. thesis, iterative methods have been used on a wide range of scientific and engineering applications with a variety of new iterative methods having been developed.

==Education and career==
Young earned a bachelor's degree in 1944 from the [[Webb Institute of Naval Architecture]]. After service in the U.S. Navy during part of World War II, he went to [[Harvard University]] to study mathematics and was awarded a master's degree in 1947 and a Ph.D in 1950, working under the supervision of Professor [[Garrett Birkhoff]]. Young began his academic career at the [[University of Maryland, College Park]] and he was the first to teach a mathematics course focusing mainly on [[numerical analysis]] and computer programming.<ref>{{citation|title=Beginning of computing and computer science at Maryland |year=2004 |first=Jack |last=Minker |url=http://www.cs.umd.edu/department/dept-history/minker-report.pdf |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110610064807/http://www.cs.umd.edu/department/dept-history/minker-report.pdf |archivedate=2011-06-10 }}.</ref> After several years working in the aero-space industry in Los Angeles, he joined the faculty of the [[University of Texas at Austin]], [[Texas]], in 1958. Young was the founding Director of the university Computation Center and then the research Center for Numerical Analysis (CNA) in 1970. He would become the [[Ashbel Smith]] [[Professor]] of Mathematics and Computer Sciences as well as a founding member of the [[Institute for Computational Engineering and Sciences]] (ICES), all at the University of Texas at Austin.

==Awards and honors==
Young was awarded the title: [[Fellow]] of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]. He was honored by the [[Association for Computing Machinery]] (ACM) in 1990 for "outstanding contributions to computer science". In October 1988, the first IMACS International Conference on Iterative Method was held in Austin, Texas, in honor of Young's 65th birthday. The book Iterative Methods for Large Linear Systems (David R. Kincaid and Linda J. Hayes, eds., Academic Press, 1990) contains the invited presentations. A special issue of the Journal of Linear Algebra and Its Applications was dedicated to Young for his 70th birthday.<ref name="nlaa95"/>  In 1998, the fourth IMACS Iterative Conference was held at the University of Texas at Austin in special recognition of Young's 75th birthday and [[Richard S. Varga|Richard Varga]]'s 70th birthday. In 2000, a symposium was given at the [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|SIAM]] Annual Meeting in Puerto Rico on the occasion of the 50th anniversary of Young's publication of the SOR method.
